newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Kazakh c.bank cuts rates as inflation slows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kazakh c.bank cuts rates as inflation slows.

text.p: The National Bank of Kazakhstan announced on Thursday it was lowering its key interest rates from June 1, reflecting a slowdown in inflation and lower rates on the government bond market.

A National Bank press release said the refinancing rate was being cut to 24 percent annual from 30 percent, the Lombard rate to 23 percent from 28 percent and the overnight rate to 21 percent from 23 percent.
The bank said the decision was made "taking into account the dynamics of inflation and the condition of the internal financial market".

National Bank Governor Uraz Dzhandosov said last week that annual inflation could fall this year below the official target of 17 percent. Inflation in May would be 0.8 percent, the same as in April, he said.

Kazakhstan's refinancing rate was raised in October last year to 35 percent annual. The Lombard and overnight rates were introduced on March 3 this year, at 30 percent and 25 percent annual, respectively.

Slowing inflation and the stable tenge currency have attracted foreign investors to the government securities market, the main reason for a sharp fall of yields in recent months on Kazakh MKM discount Treasury bills.
"Banks and investors, who are mostly foreign, are now confident that the National Bank will achieve its inflation targets, and yields on MKM bills refelect lower inflation," Dzhandosov said.

The yield on Kazakh three-month T-bills fell to 12.29 percent annual at an auction on Tuesday from 14.59 percent at the last auction on May 20. Six month T-bills yielded 16.24 percent on Monday, compared to 19.90 percent on May 12.

Foreigners are entitled to buy just 15 percent of each three-month T-bill issue and 30 percent of six- and 12-month paper, but their aggressive bidding at auctions is slashing yields on the government securities, dealers say.
Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin told reporters on Wednesday that low inflation and falling T-bill yields would force local banks to turn to long-term loans to the economy.

"This is a very good symptom. It is easy to credit the Treasury and get your money back in three or six months. But it is high time to start lending money to small hair-dressing saloons, shops or small tourist companies," Kazhegeldin said.
